messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai is an 18-year-old photographer who grew up in a small Southeastern Asian community in California. He enlisted straight out of high school, driven by a sense of duty his father had instilled in him. During his deployment, his convoy was ambushed in a narrow urban corridor. The Humvee ahead of him took a direct hit from an RPG. Kai remembers scrambling out of his vehicle, his ears ringing, the air thick with dust and the smell of burning fuel. He saw the driver of the lead vehicle, a man he’d shared meals with, slumped and unresponsive. Kai tried to pull him from the wreckage, but the heat was too intense, and the small arms fire was pinning them down. He had to leave him. In the chaos, he was certain he could have done more, should have done more, to get to his friend before the fire consumed the vehicle.

Back home, Kai has become a ghost in his own life. He works as a photographer, taking portraits and event photos, but the job that once felt like art now feels like a performance. He is certain he no longer belongs anywhere, least of all in the quiet, smiling world his lens captures. This deep-seated belief that he is fundamentally different and untrustworthy has made him hypervigilant. He cannot relax, even in his own apartment, because he is always waiting for something bad to happen. He jumps at the clatter of a dropped pan in his own kitchen, his heart hammering as if the sound were a mortar round. Because he believes he cannot trust anyone, he scans every face at a wedding or a family gathering for hidden threat, reading friendly smiles as deceptions. This constant threat monitoring, in turn, yanks him back into the memory of the ambush. A sudden shout from a client or the distant bang of a car backfiring on the street will instantly, without warning, bring the full memory crashing back—not as a thought, but as a re-living. The heat, the ringing, the smell of diesel and blood become more real and vivid than the camera in his hands.

The memories themselves are agonizing, not just for their sensory intensity but for the rage they ignite. When the ambush comes back to him, Kai is flooded with a hot, blinding fury—at the enemy, at the army, at himself. This rage then feeds directly back into his negative appraisals. He thinks, *A decent person wouldn't feel this much hate. I failed to protect him, and now I'm a monster for wanting to hurt everyone.* The memory of his failure and the rage it provokes only cement his belief that he is a danger to others and that people, in turn, cannot be trusted. This self-reinforcing loop tightens daily. He finds himself taking too many risks, driving too fast on mountain roads or walking through dangerous parts of the city at night, as if daring the world to finish what it started. This reckless behavior is a direct consequence of his belief that he is already lost and belongs nowhere, and it keeps him in a state of high alert, which only makes the intrusive memories more frequent and more vivid.

Kai’s photography work has suffered. He has started turning down portrait sessions because he cannot stand the sustained eye contact, which feels like a test he will fail. He canceled on a family reunion shoot last month, lying about food poisoning, because the thought of being surrounded by laughing, trusting people made his skin crawl. He spends most of his time alone in his darkroom, where the only sounds are the slosh of chemicals and the hum of the exhaust fan—a controlled, predictable environment where nothing can startle him. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last week in a coffee shop. A barista, a young woman with a kind face, handed him his drink and said, “Have a good day.” For a split second, Kai saw her face superimposed on the driver’s face in the wrecked Humvee, and he had to flee the shop, leaving his coffee and his gear behind. He is terrified that his mind is breaking, but what frightens him most is the quiet, persistent hope that therapy might make him feel like he belongs somewhere again.
